Hans Lufft
hāns looft
n. (Hans Lufft, 1495–1584, printer of Wittenberg and of Luther's German Bible)
German Hans, a short form of Johannes, the LORD is gracious; Lufft, air, from Middle High German luft.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hans Lufft printed the German Bible. He set up at Wittenberg about 1523 and in 1534 brought out the first complete Luther Bible, the whole canon in German from the original tongues, and over the next forty years his house produced something near a hundred thousand copies of it. The figure is almost unbelievable for the sixteenth century and it is roughly what the sources support. He was called the Bible-printer in his own lifetime. He printed with care: Luther, Melanchthon and others sat as a revision committee through the 1530s and 1540s and Lufft set their corrections edition by edition, so that the text improved steadily rather than drifting. He became a prosperous man and burgomaster of Wittenberg. What a hundred thousand German Bibles did to a nation over forty years is not measurable by any method we have, and it is the largest single fact about the German Reformation after Luther himself. “The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple” (Psa 119:130).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines impression as the copies of a book printed at one time, and revision as a re-examination for correction.

IMPRES'SION, n. The copies of a book printed at one time; an edition.

REVI'SION, n. The act of reviewing; review; re-examination for correction.

CIRCULA'TION, n. The extent to which anything is diffused or spread abroad.

BUR'GOMASTER, n. The chief magistrate of a municipal town in Holland, Flanders and Germany.

Modern Corruption

A hundred thousand German Bibles out of one Wittenberg house in forty years.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the measuring of a reformation by its controversies, so that the pamphlet war and the diets fill the account and the quiet arithmetic of a press running for forty years is a footnote. Lufft's hundred thousand Bibles reached more German households than every polemical tract of the century put together, and they went on working after the controversies were cold.

The principle to recover is that the word works by its own nature and over time, which is why the Lord compares the kingdom to seed and to leaven rather than to a battle. “The kingdom of heaven is like unto leaven, which a woman took, and hid in three measures of meal, till the whole was leavened” (Mat 13:33). The guarantee attached to the sending is unconditional: “it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please” (Isa 55:11).
